beginner: The economy grew 2.2% last year, which is solid but not spectacular. Job market stays healthy with 4.2% unemployment, so most people looking for work can find it.
Prices are rising at 2.3% annually, which is close to the Federal Reserve's target. Your paycheck probably keeps up with inflation right now.
The government spends way more money than it collects in taxes. That 7.5% deficit means future taxpayers will foot the bill.
moderate: GDP growth of 2.2% sits below the 2.5% to 3% the US averaged before 2008, signaling a slower-growth regime. The unemployment rate of 4.2% reflects a cooling labor market compared to the sub-4% readings of 2023 and 2024.

Inflation at 2.3% suggests the Fed's aggressive rate hikes worked, though the 3.25% policy rate remains restrictive relative to nominal growth. Core inflation dynamics matter more than headline figures, and persistence in services inflation keeps policymakers cautious.

The budget deficit of 7.5% of GDP persists despite full employment and moderate growth, driven by entitlement spending and defense outlays. The current account deficit of 3.8% reflects chronic capital inflows and weak household savings rates, creating medium-term currency pressure if the Fed cuts rates.
expert: Real GDP growth of 2.2% against headline inflation of 2.3% produces near-zero real growth, well below potential output of 2.5% to 2.8%. The unemployment rate at 4.2% masks labor force participation flatness and underemployment in prime-age cohorts, suggesting slack exists despite headline tightness.

With the federal funds rate at 325 basis points and core PCE inflation running elevated in services, the Fed faces a dilemma between cutting to forestall a slowdown and holding to anchor expectations. The 7.5% fiscal deficit crowds out private investment and widens the current account deficit to 3.8% of GDP, both structural headwinds to sustainable growth.

Forward guidance hinges on the Treasury yield curve and mortgage rate transmission; a sustained inversion and higher term premia could trigger demand destruction faster than base case forecasts. If the current account deficit persists above 3.5% while the budget deficit remains elevated, foreign central bank Treasury demand becomes critical to containing long-end yields and preventing a dollar depreciation spiral that reignites import price inflation.

beginner: Canada's economy grew just 1.7% last year, slower than the US. That means fewer new jobs, and unemployment sits at 6.5%, which is noticeably higher.
Inflation in Canada is 2%, right at the Bank of Canada's comfort zone. Living costs are stable, which is good news for household budgets.
Canada's government runs a much smaller deficit than the US, at just 1.5% of GDP. The country also has a nearly balanced current account, meaning it doesn't rely on foreign borrowing.
moderate: Growth of 1.7% trails the US by 0.5 percentage points, reflecting weakness in commodity exports and muted domestic consumption. The unemployment rate of 6.5% is the highest among G7 peers, signaling persistent labor market softness despite subdued inflation.

Inflation at 2% sits bang on target, but the Bank of Canada cut rates to 2.25% because growth is too weak to absorb slack productively. The current account is nearly balanced at negative 0.5% of GDP, a structural improvement from the 2010s.

The budget deficit of 1.5% is sustainable and reflects fiscal constraint relative to the US. Canadian household debt remains elevated, so the rate cuts may support asset prices rather than broad-based demand recovery.
expert: Real GDP growth of 1.7% against 2% inflation produces declining real incomes, while the unemployment rate at 6.5% has risen 110 basis points from cycle lows in 2022. Labor force participation fell sharply in late 2025, masking underlying slack in the prime-age cohort.

The Bank of Canada's 2.25% policy rate reflects aggressive easing (75 basis points of cuts since mid-2024) aimed at supporting demand, but transmission lags and household debt serviceability constraints limit stimulus efficacy. The budget deficit of 1.5% of GDP provides modest fiscal support, while the current account deficit of 0.5% is sustainable but reflects lower commodity export demand.

Forward growth depends on whether rate cuts trigger household consumption (consumption spending fell 0.3% in Q4 2025) and whether commodity prices stabilize; if oil remains below USD 65 per barrel, energy sector capex will remain depressed. The Bank of Canada faces a dilemma between further cuts (risking currency depreciation) and holding steady (risking persistent unemployment above the NAIRU of 5%).

beginner: The UK economy grew 1.5% last year, slower than the US and Canada. Growth has been sluggish since Brexit, and it shows.
Inflation is 2.1%, just above the Bank of England's 2% target. Prices are stable enough that the average person isn't squeezed.
Unemployment is 5%, which means the job market is tight but not overheated. The government runs a 4.2% deficit, which is moderate but not small.
moderate: Growth of 1.5% reflects persistent Brexit-related structural headwinds that have shaved 4% from potential GDP relative to pre-2016 trends. Unemployment at 5% masks significant regional disparities, with Northern England and Wales experiencing unemployment above 6%.

Inflation at 2.1% is just above target, but the Bank of England holds rates at 3.5% because underlying services inflation remains sticky and wage growth at 5% outpaces productivity gains. The current account deficit of 2.5% reflects weak export competitiveness tied to reduced trade with the EU.

The budget deficit of 4.2% of GDP is driven by elevated public sector employment costs and weak corporate tax receipts. The Office for Budget Responsibility projects the deficit will widen absent fiscal tightening, pressuring gilts if investors grow impatient.
expert: Real GDP growth of 1.5% against inflation of 2.1% produces persistent real income declines, while unemployment at 5% sits above most economists' estimates of the NAIRU (4.5%), suggesting demand softness despite wage growth. The labor force participation rate fell 0.3 percentage points in the past year, driven by early retirements and long-term sick leave.

The Bank of England's 3.5% policy rate provides real restraint, yet gilt yields at the long end trade above 3.8% due to fiscal concern and supply dynamics. The current account deficit of 2.5% of GDP widened from 2% in 2024, reflecting a deterioration in goods trade (down 8% year-over-year) offsetting gains in services exports.

Forward outlook depends on two offsetting forces: rate cuts (forecast at 300 basis points by end-2026) could support property and consumption, but the budget deficit at 4.2% of GDP crowds out private investment and signals fiscal consolidation risk. If gilt yields exceed 4.5% in the next six months due to hawkish central bank communications or supply shocks, refinancing costs for the government will accelerate and constrain counter-cyclical support, deepening the growth shortfall versus peers.

beginner: Japan's economy grew only 0.8% last year, the slowest among major economies. Aging population and low immigration mean fewer young workers, which limits growth.
Inflation is 1.8%, below the Bank of Japan's 2% target. The Bank of Japan raised rates to 1.25% but remains accommodative compared to other central banks.
Japan has a 4.8% current account surplus, meaning the country saves more than it spends. This makes Japan a net lender to the world, which strengthens the yen.
moderate: Growth of 0.8% reflects structural headwinds tied to demographic contraction, with the working-age population shrinking 0.7% annually and productivity gains too weak to offset. The unemployment rate of 2.5% is the lowest in the G7 but masks chronic underemployment in part-time and gig work.

Inflation at 1.8% sits persistently below the Bank of Japan's 2% target despite tight labor markets, reflecting anchored expectations and weak wage growth outside manufacturing. The policy rate at 1.25% moved higher in late 2025, but real rates remain negative at negative 0.55%, indicating continued monetary accommodation.

The current account surplus of 4.8% of GDP is the largest globally, driven by persistent trade surpluses in electronics and autos despite weak domestic demand. The budget deficit of 1.2% of GDP masks a primary deficit of negative 0.8%, meaning the government covers operating costs through borrowing despite nominally low deficits.
expert: Real GDP growth of 0.8% against 1.8% inflation produces deteriorating real incomes, while unemployment at 2.5% masks an effective NAIRU near 2.8% given persistent wage moderation. Labor force participation declined 0.2 percentage points in 2025 as early retirements outpaced immigration inflows.

The Bank of Japan's 1.25% policy rate and negative real rates reflect a regime where the central bank tolerates inflation undershooting (1.8% vs 2% target) to support asset prices and growth. The current account surplus of 4.8% of GDP is structurally stable, but yen appreciation pressure from carry-trade unwinds in 2024-2025 has reversed, creating currency volatility.

Forward growth depends critically on whether structural reforms (labor market liberalization, immigration expansion, capex incentives) raise potential output above 1%, else Japan risks secular stagnation despite fiscal stimulus. If inflation remains below 2% and the Bank of Japan holds real rates negative through 2026, portfolio flows may shift toward higher-yielding assets abroad, pressuring the yen and importing inflation via import prices; this transmission mechanism is the only near-term lever for demand creation in a demand-constrained, demographic-shrinking economy.

beginner: Germany's economy grew just 1.2% last year, which is slow compared to most other countries. Your paycheck probably isn't keeping up with inflation.
The jobless rate sits at 3.8%, meaning most people who want work can find it. This is one of Europe's strongest job markets.
Germany runs a huge surplus with other countries (4.5% of GDP), meaning it exports way more than it imports. German companies are doing well selling abroad.
moderate: Germany expanded 1.2% while inflation cooled to 2.2%, but this growth lags France's 1.4% and trails pre-pandemic performance. The ECB keeps rates at 2.50%, offering little stimulus to rev up demand.
Unemployment at 3.8% reflects Germany's stronger labor market compared to France's 7.7%, though both face aging workforces. Germany's manufacturing sector remains a ballast.

The 4.5% current account surplus signals German competitiveness, yet the 2% budget deficit (smallest in the eurozone) hints at fiscal caution when growth needs a boost. Export dependence leaves Germany vulnerable to global demand shocks.
expert: Germany posted 1.2% growth against 2.2% inflation and 3.8% unemployment, but the 2% budget deficit represents fiscal drag during a period when private investment demand remains tepid. The ECB's 2.50% policy rate sits neutral to slightly restrictive in nominal terms.

The 4.5% current account surplus masks structural challenges: aging demographics compress domestic demand while manufacturing competitiveness relies on wage moderation rather than productivity gains. France's higher deficit-to-GDP ratio (4.8%) reflects more expansionary fiscal stance.

Germany's 1.2% growth trajectory, anchored by a 4.5% current account surplus and 3.8% unemployment, suggests the economy operates near trend with limited slack. Forward guidance hinges on whether eurozone demand stabilizes or whether China's slowdown (4.7% growth versus historical 6%+ levels) triggers another export contraction.

beginner: France grew 1.4% last year, slightly better than Germany but still quite slow. Prices rose 2%, so your savings are losing value.
France has a bigger jobs problem than Germany, with 7.7% unemployed versus Germany's 3.8%. This means more French people are struggling to find work.
France spends more than it takes in, running a deficit of 4.8% of GDP. The government is borrowing heavily to fund programs.
moderate: France nudged ahead of Germany with 1.4% growth while keeping inflation at 2%, but the 7.7% unemployment rate is double Germany's and reveals persistent labor market weakness. Fiscal spending at 4.8% deficit-to-GDP shows the government tried to support demand.

France's current account stays barely positive at 1%, unlike Germany's 4.5% surplus, reflecting weaker export competitiveness and stronger import demand. The budget deficit ranks among Europe's highest outside crisis periods.

Youth unemployment and regional disparities drive France's 7.7% headline rate, a structural headwind that fiscal stimulus alone cannot fix. The ECB holds rates at 2.50% across the eurozone, meaning France cannot engineer independent monetary relief.
expert: France achieved 1.4% growth with 2% inflation and a 7.7% unemployment rate while running a 4.8% budget deficit, the highest in the eurozone sample. This combination signals fiscal support masking weak underlying demand and poor labor market dynamics.

The 1% current account position sits fragile relative to historical norms, with France's trade balance deteriorating as imports of capital goods exceed export gains. The 4.8% deficit reflects both cyclical support and structural spending commitments that constrain fiscal space.

France's unemployment-to-growth ratio suggests policymakers face a trilemma: 1.4% growth cannot absorb labor supply, the 4.8% deficit crowds out private investment, and the ECB's unified 2.50% rate offers no relief for zone-specific weakness. Watch for wage pressures if labor markets tighten despite slow growth.

beginner: Italy's economy grew just 1% last year, the slowest in this group. This weak growth means fewer new jobs and less opportunity for workers.
Unemployment in Italy sits at 5.6%, better than France but worse than Germany. Prices rose 2.3%, the highest inflation among these countries.
Italy borrows money at 3.2% of GDP in deficit spending. This adds to Italy's already large government debt, the second highest in Europe.
moderate: Italy expanded at only 1% while inflation reached 2.3% (the group's high), and unemployment of 5.6% remains elevated versus Germany but better than France. The 3.2% budget deficit reflects ongoing structural fiscal challenges.

Italy's 0.8% current account surplus is modest, signaling balanced trade but limited export dynamism compared to Germany's 4.5%. The combination of slow growth and persistent debt ratios constrains future fiscal flexibility.

Youth unemployment in Italy runs substantially higher than headline rates, with the 1% growth rate insufficient to absorb new entrants into the labor force. The 3.2% deficit-to-GDP supports demand but lacks room for bold expansion given debt stocks exceeding 140% of GDP.
expert: Italy logged 1% growth, 2.3% inflation (highest in sample), 5.6% unemployment, and a 3.2% budget deficit while maintaining a 0.8% current account position. The inflation premium over eurozone peers signals wage or import price pressures despite anemic demand growth.

The 0.8% current account surplus masks compositional weakness in manufactured exports, with services and tourism providing the margin. The 3.2% deficit reflects both cyclical support and structural transfers that leave little space for discretionary fiscal expansion.

Italy's 1% growth trajectory, combined with 2.3% inflation and 3.2% deficit, indicates the economy operates below potential while fiscal constraints tighten. Watch for political pressure on the ECB's 2.50% rate as Italian debt service costs rise and unemployment fails to fall with growth.

beginner: China grew 4.7% last year, much faster than any European country. This rapid growth means more jobs and rising living standards for millions of Chinese workers.
China's unemployment sits at 5.1% and inflation at 2%, both moderate levels. The government is spending heavily with a 6.8% budget deficit to keep growth strong.
China runs a trade surplus of 2.5% of GDP, meaning it exports more than it imports. This money flowing in helps fund growth.
moderate: China expanded 4.7%, nearly four times Germany's pace, while inflation stayed flat at 2% and unemployment held at 5.1%. The 6.8% budget deficit shows Beijing deployed massive fiscal support to reach these targets.

China's current account surplus of 2.5% differs sharply from European patterns, reflecting export-led growth and capital controls that limit outflows. The fiscal deficit at 6.8% represents stimulus comparable to crisis periods in the West, signaling authorities view underlying momentum as fragile.

China's policy rate of 2.75% sits 25 basis points above the ECB's 2.50%, yet real rates remain deeply negative given inflation dynamics and credit growth targets. The 6.8% deficit-to-GDP ratio masks off-budget spending through state-owned enterprises and local governments.
expert: China delivered 4.7% growth against 2% inflation and 5.1% unemployment while running a 6.8% budget deficit and maintaining a 2.5% current account surplus. The fiscal injection suggests authorities accepted below-trend growth as baseline and deployed stimulus to defend 5% thresholds.

The 2.75% policy rate and 2% inflation imply a real rate of roughly 75 basis points, but shadow lending rates and implicit subsidies to strategic sectors compress effective borrowing costs well below nominal policy rates. The 2.5% current account surplus, down from 3%+ pre-pandemic levels, reflects both structural rebalancing and weaker global demand for Chinese exports.

China's 4.7% growth anchored by 6.8% fiscal support and maintained current account surplus signals the economy has shifted to policy-dependent expansion rather than export-led dynamism. Forward momentum depends on whether fiscal multipliers hold and whether shadow banking deleveraging compounds amid property sector weakness.

beginner: India's economy grew 6.3% last year, faster than most other big countries. That means more jobs and higher incomes for ordinary people.
Prices are rising at 4.2%, which is moderate. Your money buys slightly less than it did a year ago, but not dramatically so.
The government is spending more than it collects in taxes. This means less money available for roads, schools, and hospitals down the road.
moderate: India expanded 6.3% annually, well above the global average of 2.5% but cooling from 7.2% two years ago. Growth remains robust despite global headwinds, though it's slowing from its earlier trajectory.

Inflation at 4.2% sits near the central bank's 4% target, giving policymakers room to hold rates steady at 6%. This stability contrasts sharply with Brazil's 12% and Russia's 12%, where inflation pressures forced aggressive tightening.
The budget deficit reached 7.2% of GDP, one of the highest among emerging markets. This fiscal expansion funded infrastructure and social programs but leaves limited cushion if revenues weaken.
expert: India's 6.3% growth rate masks diverging sectoral performance, with services and IT offsetting agricultural weakness from erratic monsoons. The unemployment rate of 4.7% represents formal sector tightness, but underemployment in rural areas and the informal sector remains substantial at roughly 27% of the workforce.

CPI inflation of 4.2% pins policy rates at 6%, creating negative real rates of roughly 1.8% and signaling the RBI retains easing optionality if growth decelerates. The current account deficit of 1.2% of GDP, manageable by historical standards, reflects robust import demand tied to capex cycles.

Forward indicators suggest growth may moderate to 5.5-6% in 2026-27 as base effects fade and global demand softens. The fiscal deficit trajectory poses medium-term risks if coupled with external shocks, given limited policy space to absorb commodity price spikes or capital flow reversals.

beginner: South Africa's economy barely grew last year at just 1.5%. That's slower than inflation, meaning most people are getting poorer.
Unemployment is stuck at 32.5%, among the worst in the world. Almost one in three people looking for work can't find a job.
Prices are stable at 3.5%, which is good news for your wallet. But this low inflation reflects weak demand, not a healthy economy.
moderate: South Africa expanded only 1.5% annually, less than half its pre-pandemic rate and trailing even stagnant developed economies. Load shedding, skills mismatches, and state-owned enterprise dysfunction choke potential growth.

Unemployment reached 32.5%, the highest globally among comparable economies and representing roughly 6.7 million jobless. Youth unemployment exceeds 60%, signaling a lost generation of workforce participation.

Inflation at 3.5% is tame but reflects demand collapse rather than policy success. The central bank holds rates at 6.25%, the highest among emerging markets excluding Brazil and Russia, yet real rates remain contractionary given economic slack.
expert: South Africa's 1.5% growth reflects structural constraints: electricity capacity utilization below 50%, logistics costs 40% above regional peers, and mining sector contraction amid commodity price softness. The unemployment rate of 32.5% understates slack, as broad unemployment (including discouraged workers) approaches 42%.

CPI at 3.5% masks service-sector inflation near 5.5% offset by goods deflation, indicating demand destruction. Real policy rates at 2.75% leave the SARB little room to ease despite recession risks, constrained by currency fragility and current account deficits of 1.4% of GDP.

The fiscal deficit of 4.8% of GDP, while moderate by regional standards, compounds under low growth, driving public debt above 70% of GDP. Near-term catalysts depend entirely on electricity infrastructure recovery and fiscal consolidation credibility, both politically fraught and likely to disappoint through 2026.

beginner: Brazil's economy grew just 1.7% last year, barely keeping up with inflation at 4.2%. Most Brazilians aren't seeing meaningful income gains.
Unemployment is 5.7%, reasonable on paper but wages aren't keeping up with rising prices. Your paycheck doesn't go as far as it used to.
The central bank raised interest rates to 12% to fight inflation. This makes borrowing expensive for mortgages, cars, and business loans.
moderate: Brazil expanded 1.7% annually, lagging Mexico (3.2%) and even Argentina's modest recovery. Agricultural exports remain strong, but manufacturing weakness and public sector retrenchment drag broader momentum.

Inflation at 4.2% prompted the central bank to hike aggressively to 12%, the highest in the region and approaching 2015 levels. The real interest rate of 7.8% is contractionary, signaling the Fed now prioritizes inflation targeting over growth support.

The current account deficit ballooned to 2.6% of GDP, driven by profit repatriation and manufactured goods imports despite commodity tailwinds. Brazil's budget is nearly balanced at 0.8%, the most disciplined in emerging markets, but monetary tightness is the binding constraint on growth.
expert: Brazil's 1.7% growth contrasts with its potential 2.5-3% trend, with manufacturing PMIs below 50 signaling contraction and agricultural output vulnerable to La Niña. Unemployment at 5.7% masks underemployment near 10%, concentrated in informal sectors where wage pressures remain acute despite headline restraint.

The central bank's 12% policy rate, lifted from 10.5% in late 2025, targets CPI at 4.2% from above its 3% midpoint. Real rates of 7.8% represent the highest tightening cycle since 2015-16, destroying capex demand despite moderate deficit financing of 0.8% of GDP.

Forward guidance suggests the Banco Central will hold at 12% through mid-2026 if CPI remains sticky above 4%, creating a growth recession scenario where unemployment drifts toward 6.5%. The current account deficit of 2.6% of GDP, while manageable given commodity buffers, constrains policy flexibility if capital flows reverse on global rate volatility.

beginner: Russia's economy grew just 0.9%, the slowest among major emerging markets. Sanctions, war spending, and isolation from Western trade are taking a toll.
The central bank hiked rates to 12% to fight inflation at 4.7%. Very high rates make it expensive for families and businesses to borrow.
Russia actually exports more than it imports, so money is flowing in. This comes from oil and gas sales, but it masks a struggling domestic economy.
moderate: Russia expanded only 0.9% annually, constrained by military spending of roughly 6% of GDP, capital flight, and sanctions-induced import substitution inefficiencies. Growth is near stall speed despite a current account surplus, unusual among peers.

Inflation at 4.7% sits above the central bank's 4% target, prompting rates of 12% to cool demand. This is deliberate policy to prevent overheating amid tight labor markets (unemployment 2.5%) and wage pressures from military conscription.

The current account surplus of 2% of GDP is anomalous for emerging markets and reflects trade restructuring: lower imports (capital goods scarce), sustained energy exports, and remittance outflows partially offsetting. Budget deficits of 2.5% of GDP finance defense, but capital controls limit external financing needs.
expert: Russia's 0.9% growth masks a dual economy: traded sectors (oil, gas, metals) relatively healthy while non-traded sectors contract under demand destruction. Unemployment of 2.5% is artificially low due to military absorption and statistical manipulation, while effective unemployment including underutilized labor likely exceeds 6%.

CPI inflation at 4.7%, above the 4% target despite a 12% policy rate, suggests core pressures remain sticky from wage growth (near 9% annually) driven by conscription-driven labor scarcity. Real policy rates of 7.3% are contractionary, yet the Banco Central signaled further hikes if inflation breaches 5%, risking growth destruction.

The current account surplus of 2% of GDP, unprecedented for a major emerging economy in contraction, reflects trade composition shifts and capital flight masking underlying external imbalances. Forward guidance points to policy rates staying above 11% through 2026 if geopolitical risks elevate, locking in stagflation dynamics where growth slides toward zero while inflation proves sticky above 5%.

expert.body: <cite index="22-1,23-3,24-5">The IEA's unanimous approval of a 400 million barrel emergency release dwarfs the 182.7 million barrel response to Russia's Ukraine invasion, yet markets remain skeptical</cite>. <cite index="26-4,26-13,30-8">WTI crude briefly dipped below session lows after the announcement before climbing back above $88, with Brent trading over $90</cite>. <cite index="29-6,29-8">Export volumes through the Strait of Hormuz have collapsed to less than 10% of pre-conflict levels, disrupting 20 million barrels per day that normally transit the waterway</cite>. <cite index="26-19,28-17">JPMorgan notes that U.S. SPR releases typically take 13 days to begin delivery, while physical flow limits constrain how quickly stockpiles can be emptied</cite>. <cite index="30-9,28-19">The release equals just four days of global production and cannot substitute for restoring Strait access, according to analysts</cite>.

expert.body: <cite index="11-10,11-12,18-7,18-10">February's 0.3% monthly CPI gain and 2.4% annual rate matched consensus precisely, with core CPI at 0.2% monthly and 2.5% annually, near 2021 lows</cite>. <cite index="11-6,11-7,11-8">The Carson Group's Varghese characterized this as 'calm before the storm,' noting tariff impacts on core goods and persistent services inflation outside housing</cite>. <cite index="18-8,18-9,20-35">Shelter contributed the largest monthly increase at 0.2%, while gasoline rose 0.8% and food gained 0.4%</cite>. <cite index="11-9,20-32,8-8">The data predates the Iran conflict oil shock, with the EU warning inflation could exceed 3% if Brent sustains $100/barrel levels</cite>. <cite index="11-5,2-2,20-38">Fed funds futures price a March hold at 3.5%-3.75% with near-100% odds, as the FOMC maintains data-dependent policy amid divisions on easing pace</cite>.
